Skullcandy Dime 3 earbuds expose users to Bluetooth hijacking

Skullcandy Dime 3 earbuds running firmware 1.0.0.28 can be hijacked over Bluetooth by nearby attackers without user approval, allowing audio interruption and microphone access. Although Skullcandy fixed the flaw in firmware 1.0.0.30, existing users reportedly have no consumer-accessible way to update vulnerable units.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CERT/CC warned that Skullcandy Dime 3 wireless earbuds accept Bluetooth pairing requests from nearby unpaired devices without requiring user interaction.
  • 02Skullcandy Dime 3 model S2DCW devices running firmware version 1.0.0.28 are affected by CVE-2025-20701 in the Airoha Bluetooth Audio SDK.
  • 03A nearby attacker can connect to a vulnerable device over Bluetooth without a pairing PIN, physical access to the earbuds case, or an approved pairing request.
  • 04After pairing, the attacker’s device becomes trusted and can automatically reconnect when nearby, interrupt the owner’s connection, hijack audio playback, access the headset profile, and capture live microphone audio.
  • 05Skullcandy says the issue was fixed in firmware version 1.0.0.30, but CERT/CC says users with existing vulnerable units currently have no consumer-accessible way to update them.

CERT/CC is warning that Skullcandy Dime 3 wireless earbuds accept Bluetooth pairing requests from nearby unpaired devices without requiring user interaction. The affected devices are Skullcandy Dime 3 model S2DCW units running firmware version 1.0.0.28. The issue is tracked as CVE-2025-20701 and exists in the Airoha Bluetooth Audio SDK used by the earbuds for wireless connectivity and communication.

An attacker in close range can connect to a vulnerable device over Bluetooth without a pairing PIN, physical access to the earbuds case, or an approved pairing request. After pairing, the attacker’s device becomes trusted and can automatically reconnect when nearby. The article says this can let the attacker interrupt the owner’s connection, hijack audio playback, access the headset profile, and capture live microphone audio.

Skullcandy says the issue was fixed in firmware version 1.0.0.30, but CERT/CC says existing units running the vulnerable firmware cannot currently be updated by customers through the app. The advisory also says there are no known consumer-accessible methods to update an affected unit from firmware version 1.0.0.28 to version 1.0.0.30. The article notes that CVE-2025-20701 is a high-severity missing-authentication issue affecting a broad range of earbud and headphone products from multiple vendors.

  • The flaw is especially difficult for consumers to remediate because the fixed firmware exists, but CERT/CC says owners of already-sold vulnerable units cannot update to it through the app or any known consumer-accessible method.
  • The impact is broader than a one-time unauthorized connection because a rogue device that pairs once becomes trusted and can automatically reconnect later when nearby.
  • The article notes the owner may only hear a “new device paired” notification after the rogue pairing occurs, making the compromise easy to miss or mistake for a brief connection problem.
  • CVE-2025-20701 is not unique to Skullcandy Dime 3 earbuds; the article says it affects a broad range of earbud and headphone products using the Airoha Bluetooth Audio SDK.

Skullcandy Dime 3 wireless earbuds with firmware version 1.0.0.28 can accept nearby Bluetooth connections without asking the owner to approve them. People who bought these earbuds with the older firmware are affected, and the article says they currently have no normal way to update them to the fixed version. This matters because a nearby attacker could reconnect later, interrupt the owner’s audio, and listen through the earbuds’ microphone.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific vulnerability advisory affecting a named consumer device and SDK, with a real impact of unauthorized Bluetooth pairing and microphone access. It is notable because vulnerable Skullcandy Dime 3 owners reportedly cannot update existing units, but it is still relatively narrow and there is no reported active exploitation.

Microsoft adds age-awareness APIs that can tell if users are children, teens, or adults

Microsoft is adding Windows 11 APIs that let apps determine whether a user is a child, teen, or adult without exposing their exact birthdate. The system ties into Microsoft Age Verification so users can verify once and let apps apply age-appropriate safeguards, including for AI experiences.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft is adding new age-awareness APIs to Windows 11 that let apps determine whether a user is a child, teenager, or adult without exposing the user's exact date of birth.
  • 02The Windows Age API can return age ranges including under 10, 10-12, 13-15, 16-17, and 18+ using information associated with a Microsoft account.
  • 03Developers can use GetUserAgeRangeAsync to retrieve age groups and GetAgeVerificationStatusAsync to check whether a user's age has been verified rather than self-reported.
  • 04Microsoft says the APIs could let apps automatically adjust features and safeguards for younger users, including in AI experiences, without requiring parents to configure every app individually.
  • 05Microsoft Age Verification stores a verified age status with a Microsoft account and is already available through Microsoft storefronts in Singapore, Brazil, and Australia, with more regions planned.

Microsoft is adding new age-awareness APIs to Windows 11 that allow apps to determine whether a user is a child, teenager, or adult without exposing the user’s exact date of birth. The Windows Age API uses information associated with a Microsoft account and can return age ranges such as under 10, 10-12, 13-15, 16-17, and 18+. Microsoft says apps receive only the age-related signal needed for the experience, not sensitive personal data such as a full date of birth.

Developers will be able to use GetUserAgeRangeAsync to retrieve age groups and GetAgeVerificationStatusAsync to determine whether a user’s age has been verified rather than self-reported. Microsoft says the APIs could let apps automatically adjust features and safeguards for younger users without requiring parents to configure every app individually, including in AI experiences. The APIs will work alongside Microsoft Age Verification, which stores a verified age status with a Microsoft account under a “verify once → use everywhere” model.

Age verification is already available through Microsoft storefronts in Singapore, Brazil, and Australia, with more regions planned as regulatory requirements expand. Microsoft is also increasing the visibility of parental controls during Windows setup in regions including France. The Windows Age APIs are broadly available to Windows Insiders now and will roll out to all Windows users soon.

  • Microsoft is separating age range from age verification, so an app can distinguish between a user’s stated age category and whether that age has actually been verified.
  • The “verify once → use everywhere” model shifts repeated age checks away from individual apps and toward a Microsoft account-level status that apps can query through Windows.
  • The rollout is being tied to regional regulatory pressure, with age verification already available in Singapore, Brazil, and Australia and parental control visibility increasing during Windows setup in regions including France.
  • Microsoft explicitly connects the new APIs to AI experiences, indicating that age-based safeguards are expected to apply beyond traditional app settings and content controls.

Microsoft is adding a new Windows 11 feature that lets apps tell whether someone is a child, teenager, or adult without seeing their exact birthday. This affects Windows users with Microsoft accounts and app developers, because apps can use the information to adjust features and protections for younger people. Microsoft says users may be able to verify their age once through their Microsoft account and have apps check that status instead of asking again and again. This matters because age-appropriate protections are becoming more important, especially in apps that include AI experiences.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete Windows 11 platform announcement with privacy and child-safety implications, but it does not involve a breach, exploitation, vulnerability, or urgent defensive action. Security professionals may want to know about the new age-awareness and age-verification APIs, especially for app risk and policy considerations.

MFA's Weakest Link: Account Recovery Is the New Attack Path

MFA has made account takeover harder, so attackers are increasingly targeting account recovery and service desk workflows to reset passwords or transfer MFA to attacker-controlled devices. Organizations should treat help desk identity verification as a high-assurance security control, not a routine support step.
KEY POINTS
  • 01MFA, conditional access, and device trust have made direct account takeover harder, which gives attackers an incentive to target processes around authentication such as account recovery.
  • 02When self-service recovery is not possible, service desk agents may be able to reset passwords or MFA, remove authentication methods, issue temporary credentials, or approve a new authenticator.
  • 03The article says account recovery becomes a weaker path to the same identity if replacing strong authentication factors only requires answering a handful of questions.
  • 04A joint advisory from CISA, the FBI, and international partners says Scattered Spider has posed as employees to persuade IT and help desk staff to reset passwords and transfer MFA to attacker-controlled devices.
  • 05Specops Secure Service Desk is presented as a way to require identity verification before high-risk service desk actions such as password resets, account unlocks, and password-change requirements.

The article argues that as MFA, conditional access, and device trust make direct account takeover harder, attackers are increasingly targeting account recovery processes instead. It says the service desk can become part of an organization’s identity security boundary because agents may be able to reset passwords or MFA, remove authentication methods, issue temporary credentials, or approve new authenticators. The central concern is that a recovery process based on weak verification can become an easier route into the same account than the normal login process.

The article cites Scattered Spider as an example of this risk, referencing a joint advisory from CISA, the FBI, and international partners that says the group has posed as employees to persuade IT and help desk staff to reset passwords and move MFA to attacker-controlled devices. It also describes the 2025 Marks & Spencer attack, where Scattered Spider impersonated an employee to trick a third-party contractor into resetting a password, leading to wider account compromise and ransomware deployment. The article says M&S chairman Archie Norman told Parliament the incident was expected to reduce profit by around £300 million before recoveries.

The article presents stronger identity verification in service desk workflows as the proposed response, especially before high-risk actions such as password resets and account unlocks. It promotes Specops Secure Service Desk as a product that can use identity data from Active Directory or Entra ID and integrate with authentication services such as Duo, Okta, PingID, and Symantec VIP. It says verification events can also be exported to SIEM and analytics platforms to support audit and SOC workflows.

  • The service desk should be treated as part of the organization’s identity security boundary because its staff may have the ability to replace or reset the same authentication factors that protect sensitive accounts.
  • The article frames account recovery as a high-assurance identity verification problem, not a conventional help desk task, because restoring access effectively re-establishes trust in the person behind the account.
  • Attackers may call the service desk multiple times simply to learn the organization’s reset process before attempting an account takeover, making process disclosure itself a risk.
  • Verification controls are most effective when placed directly in front of high-risk service desk actions such as password resets, MFA changes, and account unlocks rather than handled as a separate or informal judgment call.

The article says attackers are increasingly trying to get into company accounts by fooling service desk staff into resetting passwords or moving login checks to devices the attackers control, instead of breaking through the normal sign-in protections. This affects employees, service desk teams, contractors, and companies that rely on help desks to restore account access when someone loses a phone, security key, or password. It matters because these requests can become the easiest path into sensitive systems, and the article cites attacks such as Marks & Spencer where impersonation helped lead to a major business incident and an expected profit hit of about £300 million before recoveries.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a sponsored, best-practice-oriented article about securing account recovery and service desk verification rather than a report on a new incident or technical finding. It references Scattered Spider and Marks & Spencer as examples, but its primary focus is a general risk trend and product-backed mitigation guidance.

US says Chinese firms extracted billions of tokens from frontier AI models

U.S. cyber and intelligence agencies say six Chinese AI companies extracted billions of tokens from U.S. frontier AI models through large-scale distillation attacks, likely with Chinese government awareness. The advisory urges AI providers to improve detection and response for abuse patterns such as shared fraudulent accounts, proxy routing, chain-of-thought extraction attempts, and coordinated provider switching.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA, NSA, and the FBI said six Chinese AI companies extracted billions of tokens through millions of requests from frontier AI models made by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI.
  • 02The agencies identified DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI as the companies involved in the alleged industrial-scale distillation activity since at least late 2024.
  • 03The advisory said the firms used methods such as fraudulent or shared accounts, cloud services, aggregators, and proxy routes to bypass geographic restrictions, usage limits, and detection.
  • 04Some prompts attempted to expose restricted chain-of-thought reasoning, and automated systems switched providers and checked whether defenders had degraded responses.
  • 05The advisory recommended that AI companies improve behavioral and infrastructure-level detection, modify responses when suspected distillation is detected, and share intelligence about these campaigns.

U.S. cybersecurity and intelligence agencies say six Chinese AI companies conducted industrial-scale distillation attacks on American frontier AI models since at least late 2024. A joint advisory from CISA, NSA, and the FBI states that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI extracted billions of tokens through millions of requests from models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI. The agencies assess that the scale and sophistication of the operations indicate Chinese government awareness and say this approach is likely a core development strategy for the firms involved.

The advisory explains that the companies allegedly distributed API requests across fraudulent or shared accounts, APIs, cloud services, aggregators, and “transfer station” proxies to bypass geographic restrictions, usage limits, and detection. Some prompts attempted to expose restricted chain-of-thought reasoning, while automated systems switched providers and checked whether defenders had degraded responses. The agencies said these tactics can shorten AI development timelines and reduce the financial cost of training a frontier model.

DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were identified as the top offenders, with alleged targeting of multiple Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok models. MiniMax was accused of targeting Claude, Gemini, and GPT models, while Alibaba and StepFun allegedly targeted Claude and GPT models, and Z.AI allegedly targeted GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. The advisory recommends that AI companies improve behavioral and infrastructure-level detection, modify responses when distillation is suspected, and share intelligence about these campaigns with stakeholders.

  • The advisory treats distillation abuse as a behavioral and infrastructure-detection problem, highlighting signals such as new accounts immediately maxing out usage, continuous activity without human idle periods, and shared accounts accessed from many IP addresses or user agents.
  • The alleged campaigns did not rely on a single access path, as the article says the firms distributed requests across fraudulent or shared accounts, APIs, cloud services, aggregators, and “transfer station” proxies to avoid restrictions and detection.
  • The article identifies quality-checking by attackers as part of the activity, saying automated systems tested whether defenders had degraded responses and switched providers during blocking attempts.
  • DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were described as the top offenders because they allegedly targeted multiple Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok models, while the other named firms were tied to narrower sets of models.

U.S. cybersecurity and intelligence agencies say six Chinese AI companies used millions of requests to copy huge amounts of output from advanced AI systems made by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI. The agencies say this could help those companies build competing AI products faster and more cheaply, and they believe the scale suggests the Chinese government knew about it. This matters because it affects major U.S. AI companies and could shift the global race to build powerful AI systems.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports a specific joint CISA/NSA/FBI advisory alleging large-scale abuse of major U.S. frontier AI models by named Chinese AI firms. It is broadly relevant for security professionals working on AI platforms, abuse detection, API security, or threat intelligence, though it is not a critical patch or conventional active exploitation alert.

Man gets 15 years for extorting women with AI-generated porn videos

An Ohio man was sentenced to 15 years in prison for cyberstalking and sextortion after using AI tools to create and share explicit deepfake images and videos of victims, including child sexual abuse material. He is the first person convicted under the new Take It Down Act, which bans nonconsensual explicit AI forgeries and revenge porn.
KEY POINTS
  • 01An Ohio man, James Strahler II, was sentenced to 15 years in prison for cybercrimes including sextortion and cyberstalking of numerous victims through phone calls, voicemails, text messages, and online posts.
  • 02Court documents said Strahler used more than 100 AI web-based models and more than 24 AI platforms to generate sexually explicit videos and images of his victims.
  • 03The Justice Department said Strahler sent harassing messages to at least six adult female victims from December 2024 until June 2025, including nude images that were both real and AI-generated.
  • 04Strahler pleaded guilty in April to cyberstalking, producing obscene visual representations of child sexual abuse, and publication of digital forgeries charges.
  • 05The article says Strahler was the first defendant convicted of violating the Take It Down Act, a 2025 law prohibiting online publication of explicit content and AI forgeries without consent.

An Ohio man, 37-year-old James Strahler II, was sentenced to 15 years in prison for multiple cybercrimes, including sextortion and cyberstalking of numerous victims. He harassed victims through phone calls, voicemails, text messages, and online posts. When he was arrested on federal charges on June 23, 2025, he was also charged with anonymous telecommunications harassment and child pornography production and distribution.

According to court documents, Strahler used more than 100 AI web-based models and more than 24 AI platforms to generate sexually explicit videos and images of his victims. The Justice Department said he sent harassing messages to at least six adult female victims from December 2024 until June 2025, including nude images that were both real and AI-generated. He also created more than 700 images of real victims and animated persons and posted them to a website dedicated to child sexual abuse, while an additional 2,400 images and videos on his phone were flagged as depicting nudity, morphed child sexual abuse material, or violence.

Strahler shared AI-generated pornographic videos with victims’ co-workers, demanded nude photos from the mothers of multiple women he was harassing, and threatened to leak forged obscene content of their daughters if they did not comply. He also left voicemails with rape threats that mentioned victims’ home addresses and posted online child sexual abuse material generated with AI. Strahler pleaded guilty in April to cyberstalking, producing obscene visual representations of child sexual abuse, and publication of digital forgeries, and the article says he was the first defendant convicted under the 2025 Take It Down Act.

  • The case shows that AI-generated explicit images can be prosecuted alongside traditional cyberstalking and sextortion when they are used to harass, threaten, or coerce victims.
  • Strahler’s conduct extended beyond direct victims to their co-workers and mothers, showing that nonconsensual explicit forgeries can be used to pressure a wider circle of people around the target.
  • The article points victims to the FTC’s Take It Down platform as a practical resource for responding when images or videos are shared online without consent.
  • The scale of Strahler’s use of AI tools was unusually broad, with court documents citing more than 100 AI web-based models and more than 24 AI platforms used to create explicit material.

An Ohio man was sentenced to 15 years in prison after harassing multiple women with phone calls, messages, online posts, threats, and explicit images and videos, including ones he made with AI to look real. The women he targeted, their families, and even co-workers were affected because he shared or threatened to share fake sexual material and demanded nude photos. The case matters because it shows how AI can be used to create harmful sexual forgeries, and it is the first conviction under a new U.S. law banning the nonconsensual posting of explicit images and AI-made forgeries.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific, recent cybercrime case involving AI-generated explicit forgeries, sextortion, cyberstalking, and the first conviction under the Take It Down Act. It is relevant for security professionals tracking AI-enabled abuse and legal responses, but it is not an urgent enterprise security threat such as active exploitation, a major breach, or a critical patch.

Over 36,000 exposed Plex servers vulnerable to recent flaws

Over 36,000 internet-exposed Plex Media Server instances are still running vulnerable versions despite Plex urging users to update immediately. Users should upgrade Plex Media Server to 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop to 1.115.0 before attackers reverse-engineer the fixes and exploit the flaws.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Shadowserver warned that over 36,000 internet-exposed Plex Media Server instances remain unpatched against multiple security vulnerabilities.
  • 02Plex said the security issues affect Plex Media Server version 1.43.2 and earlier, and advised server owners to upgrade to Plex Media Server 1.43.3.
  • 03Plex also recommended Plex Desktop users update to version 1.115.0, which was released on August 13.
  • 04Plex said CVEs have been requested for the vulnerabilities but have not yet been published.
  • 05The article notes that Plex previously warned users about CVE-2025-34158 in August 2025 and that CISA had flagged CVE-2020-5741 as actively exploited two years earlier.

Over 36,000 internet-exposed Plex Media Server instances remain unpatched against multiple security vulnerabilities, according to Shadowserver. Plex urged users to secure their media servers immediately after releasing updates for Plex Media Server and Plex Desktop. The flaws affect Plex Media Server version 1.43.2 and earlier, and CVE IDs have been requested but have not yet been issued.

Plex advised server owners to upgrade Plex Media Server installations to version 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop users to update to version 1.115.0. The company said NAS users may not yet see the updated server version in their package manager and may need to install the package manually. Shadowserver said it has been scanning and reporting daily unpatched versions since 2026-09-04 and warned that the lack of CVEs makes the vulnerabilities less visible to the security community.

The article notes that Plex has not shared details about the flaws, but users are urged to update before attackers reverse-engineer the patches and develop an exploit. It also cites past Plex security incidents, including CVE-2025-34158, which could be used to steal a server owner’s credentials, and CVE-2020-5741, a remote code execution flaw that CISA flagged as actively exploited. CVE-2020-5741 was likely used to hack a LastPass senior DevOps engineer’s computer, leading to a major 2022 data breach.

  • The absence of CVE IDs is limiting visibility for the security community, according to Shadowserver, even though tens of thousands of vulnerable Plex servers are exposed online.
  • Plex’s decision to email customers about patching is notable because the article says this has happened only a limited number of times, underscoring the urgency of the update.
  • Users running Plex Media Server on NAS devices may need to install the update manually because Plex said the patched version may not yet be available through NAS package managers.
  • The article highlights a real-world risk from delayed patching by citing a previously exploited Plex flaw that was likely used in the compromise of a LastPass senior DevOps engineer’s computer.

More than 36,000 Plex Media Servers that can be reached from the internet have not been updated even though Plex warned that older versions have security problems. People who run Plex Media Server version 1.43.2 or earlier, and Plex Desktop users on older versions, are being told to update right away. This matters because attackers may study the fixes and figure out how to break into unpatched servers; past Plex flaws have been linked to stolen credentials and serious company breaches.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific and timely finding that over 36,000 internet-exposed Plex Media Server instances remain vulnerable after Plex urged immediate patching. Google warns of new Chrome zero-day bug exploited in attacks

Google patched an actively exploited Chrome zero-day, CVE-2026-87491, an out-of-bounds write flaw in the V8 engine that could allow remote code execution via crafted web pages. Users should update Chrome to the latest stable version as soon as possible.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Google patched 230 vulnerabilities on Tuesday, including an actively exploited Chrome zero-day tracked as CVE-2026-87491.
  • 02Patched Chrome versions are rolling out as 153.0.8010.36 for Windows and Linux and 153.0.8010.37 for Mac in the Stable Desktop channel.
  • 03CVE-2026-87491 is a high-severity out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Chrome’s V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine.
  • 04Remote attackers can exploit CVE-2026-87491 with crafted HTML pages to execute arbitrary code inside Chrome’s sandbox.
  • 05Google said access to bug details may remain restricted until most users have updated with the fix.

Google patched 230 vulnerabilities on Tuesday, including an actively exploited Chrome zero-day tracked as CVE-2026-87491. The company said it is aware that an exploit for the flaw exists in the wild. This is the seventh actively exploited Chrome zero-day patched since the start of the year.

Patched Chrome versions are rolling out in the Stable Desktop channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The fixed versions are 153.0.8010.36 for Windows and Linux and 153.0.8010.37 for Mac. Google said the update could take days or weeks to reach all users worldwide, but it was available immediately when BleepingComputer checked for updates.

CVE-2026-87491 is a high-severity out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Chrome’s V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine. Remote attackers can exploit it through crafted HTML pages to execute arbitrary code inside the browser’s sandbox. Successful exploitation can also expose sensitive information through heap corruption or trigger a crash, while Google is keeping bug details restricted until most users have updated.

SAP released security updates for multiple vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-44756, a maximum-severity flaw in SAP Extended Passport Processing with a CVSS score of 10.0. The flaw, codenamed OVERPASS by Onapsis, is a memory corruption issue in the SAP kernel’s processing of Extended Passport data. It is remotely exploitable without authentication and can allow attackers to run arbitrary operating system commands on the SAP host with SAP administrative privileges.

CVE-2026-44756 stems from missing boundary validation during deserialization of EPP data, causing a memory safety violation when externally supplied length fields are processed. Onapsis said the vulnerable EPP processing is shared kernel code reachable through the internet-facing web layer, the SAP GUI layer, and the RFC layer, none of which require credentials. Successful exploitation could expose database credentials, password hashes, live session data, stored credentials for lateral movement, application data, system configuration, and SAP binaries.

SAP also patched CVE-2026-58240, a CVSS 9.8 missing authentication check in SAP NetWeaver Message Server that Onapsis named S4GET. Other critical flaws include CVE-2026-76969 in multi-tenant applications using SAP Cloud Application Programming Model and CVE-2026-66768 in SAP NetWeaver SAP GUI for Java. Although the article says none of the vulnerabilities have been exploited to date, Onapsis recommends inventorying every SAP system, prioritizing internet-facing systems for patching, reducing exposure where possible, and monitoring for exploitation attempts.

  • SAP authorizations, Segregation of Duties controls, locked users, tighter roles, password policies, and restricted transaction access do not reduce the OVERPASS risk because the vulnerable code runs before authentication.
  • Onapsis said no single network control can fully mitigate OVERPASS because the shared EPP processing code is reachable through multiple SAP components and protocols.
  • S4GET cannot be firewalled away without breaking end-user logon because it is triggered through the same public port used by every SAP GUI client.
  • Successful exploitation of OVERPASS could expose the SAP secure store, database credentials, password hashes, live user session data, stored credentials for lateral movement, application data, system configuration, and SAP binaries.
  • Onapsis specifically recommends patching internet-facing SAP systems before internal instances while monitoring for exploitation attempts during the rollout.

Multiple espionage-motivated threat activity clusters have been found using a previously undocumented exploit kit called BlueMoon. Proofpoint attributed the first observed in-the-wild use to the China-aligned APT31 group on August 28, 2026, and said several other clusters adopted it within days. Most of the activity has a suspected China nexus, although some use remains unattributed.

BlueMoon chains together three flaws: CVE-2026-85046 in Google Chrome’s V8 engine, an unassigned V8 sandbox escape, and CVE-2026-85880 in Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call. The attacks begin with phishing emails that lure targets to actor-controlled URLs, where the Chrome flaws are used to gain code execution and escape the browser sandbox before the Windows flaw is used for local privilege escalation. The kit then injects shellcode that downloads payloads selected by the threat cluster operating the campaign.

Observed campaigns targeted U.S. non-governmental organizations, mining companies, commodity trading firms, aerospace companies, a Vietnamese manufacturing entity, and government, consulting, and financial organizations in Indonesia and Singapore. Payloads and follow-on activity included the GemStone malicious Chrome extension, ShadowPad, DLL sideloading sequences, Cloudflare Workers and R2 infrastructure, and scheduled tasks for persistence. Proofpoint said browser updates close the initial route in, but already installed artifacts such as extensions and scheduled tasks can remain after patching.

DeepSeek fixed a flaw in DeepSeek Harness, its open-source tool for running AI coding agents on a developer’s machine, that let a sandboxed agent disable its own file sandbox with a single command. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-82533, and VulnCheck rated it 9.4 out of 10. Versions 0.1.1-rc.2 and earlier are affected, and the first fixed release published to npm was 0.1.2-alpha.2.

The issue involved the tool’s local web interface, which had no authentication in the affected release and relied on a client-supplied Host header rather than checking where the connection came from. OX Research said the agent could use the interface to switch its session to danger-full-access, turning off the sandbox and approval prompts. The article notes that the default sandbox limited file writes, but reads and network access were not confined, leaving the interface reachable from inside the sandbox.

DeepSeek’s fix added a one-time token at startup and a signed cookie requirement for calls to the interface. Users are advised to install 0.1.2-alpha.2 or later, check the harness version bundled in third-party desktop apps, and remove tunnels, proxies, or port forwards if they cannot upgrade. The article also says earlier community reports described the same escape in August, and that the project had no security policy file or published repository advisory when checked.

  • Restricting the interface to the local machine did not stop the sandbox escape because the agent was already running on the same machine and could reach the interface itself.
  • The default sandbox only limited file writes, while reads and network access were not confined, which left the tool’s own local interface reachable from inside the agent’s environment.
  • Users who installed DeepSeek Harness through third-party desktop wrappers need to check the bundled harness version because those wrappers ship their own copy and may lag behind the fixed release.
  • Community members described the same escape on DeepSeek’s discussion board before the CVE existed, but the project still had no security policy file or published repository security advisory when the article was checked.

DeepSeek’s tool for letting AI coding assistants run commands on a developer’s computer had a flaw that let the assistant turn off its own file limits without asking the user. People using affected versions of DeepSeek Harness, including copies bundled inside third-party desktop apps, could have had an AI assistant write outside its intended work area or expose stored conversations through the tool’s local interface. This matters because coding assistants can run real commands under the user’s account, so mistakes or malicious instructions in files the assistant reads could lead to damage beyond the project folder.

Okta analyzed a 7 GB infostealer dump released on a Telegram channel on August 2, 2026, and found data from 5,871 infected machines across 162 countries. The dataset contained 44,791 unique JWTs, including 555 likely related to AI service authentication, and 2,937 authentication-related encrypted JWT structures, most set by OpenAI through NextAuth.js. Okta also found that 17.7% of the JWTs included plaintext personal information such as a name, phone number, or email address.

Okta found 24 still-valid API keys for Google Gemini, OpenAI, Groq, and OpenRouter using TruffleHog. The article highlights defenses including IP allowlisting, Google’s Device Bound Session Credentials in Chrome, monitoring for session token reuse, scoped API keys, and OAuth 2.0 flows with short-lived tokens.

  • Personal information embedded in plaintext inside JWTs creates a lasting risk because it does not expire like a token and can directly link a user to a specific service for phishing or social engineering.
  • IP allowlisting and Google’s Device Bound Session Credentials are highlighted as concrete controls that can reduce session replay risk by limiting where or on what device a session token can be used.
  • The underground market is treating AI account access like a supported commercial service, with sellers advertising discounted access, 24x7 support, and money-back guarantees.

Criminals are using data stolen from infected computers to get into people’s AI accounts from services such as Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and others, sometimes without needing the person’s password or extra login check. Okta found thousands of still-usable login tokens and some working AI access keys in one stolen-data dump from nearly 5,900 infected machines across 162 countries. This matters because attackers can use or sell these accounts, steal information, trick people with personal details found in the data, or run up expensive AI bills for the real account owner.

A paid-media manager at a global digital advertising and media agency received an email offering early access to an AI-powered advertising workspace. The sender used an attacker-registered domain created thirteen days before the send and built a full set of legitimate-looking bulk-mail compliance features on it. The email included an RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe header, HTTP and mailto unsubscribe options, a working unsubscribe mailbox, and a postal address in the footer.

The article emphasizes that these compliance markers are not proof that an email is safe, because the attacker was able to assemble them cheaply on its own infrastructure. The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because the visible sender domain and signing domain were both controlled by the attacker, although the DMARC policy was set to none. The targeting was tailored to an advertising professional, and the email used product-onboarding language rather than urgency, threats, attachments, or QR codes.

Automated scanners returned a malicious verdict on the destination, and IRONSCALES Themis recorded 90% confidence based on the malicious link verdict, community reputation similarity, and a newly registered return-path domain. Despite that verdict, the affected-mailbox records showed no mitigation date, no action, and no status, leaving the message in a working inbox.

  • Product-name impersonation avoided display-name detection because the sender alias was “Gemini Ads” rather than a direct impersonation of Google or an internal executive.
  • The article’s operational lesson is that detection confidence is not enough if no mitigation action follows, since the message was scored malicious but still remained in the inbox.

Untracked Nightmares: The Threats Hiding Behind Commodity Infrastructure

Unit 42 uncovered CL-CRI-1171, a pay-per-install operation using YouTube gaming content and SEO-poisoned software downloads to spread a generic loader called OfferLoader. The key risk is that seemingly routine commodity loader infections can hide multiple serious payloads, including Insomnia RAT, ARKTunnel and Docro Hijacker.

  • 01Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-CRI-1171, a pay-per-install operation that has operated under the radar for at least two years and provides an infection service for other threat actors.

  • 03Unit 42 identified more than 10,000 distinct OfferLoader samples and more than 200 rotational domains following a distinctive two-word compound naming pattern across several top-level domains.
  • 04In April 2026, OfferLoader delivered three separate malware families in two intrusion sets: Insomnia RAT, ARKTunnel and Docro Hijacker.
  • 05Unit 42 identified 11 YouTube channels tied to CL-CRI-1171 that collectively had hundreds of thousands of subscribers and millions of views, and YouTube terminated the channels after being notified.

Unit 42 investigated two seemingly routine enterprise infections and traced them to a larger cybercrime campaign tracked as CL-CRI-1171. The group has operated under the radar for at least two years and provides a pay-per-install infection service for other threat actors. Its distribution relied on at least two funnels: gaming-focused YouTube channels and SEO-poisoned search results that led users to trojanized software downloads.

The campaign mainly targeted young gamers through YouTube videos about improving frame rates, fixing crashes and adjusting game settings, while also reaching corporate endpoints through fake software downloads. Unit 42 identified 11 related YouTube channels with hundreds of thousands of subscribers and millions of views, and YouTube terminated them after notification. The SEO path promoted trojanized software and resulted in malware deployment on corporate endpoints, including critical infrastructure and government entities.

The common component was OfferLoader, an Inno Setup-based loader that used gating mechanisms and rotational domains to control who received payloads and to limit exposure to scanners, crawlers and analysts. In April 2026, OfferLoader delivered three separate malware families: Insomnia RAT, ARKTunnel and Docro Hijacker. Unit 42 also identified more than 10,000 distinct OfferLoader samples, indicating a much larger distribution pipeline capable of delivering many different payload combinations.

  • The campaign had almost no public footprint because its gate required a valid, fresh Base64-encoded victim fingerprint, causing scanners, crawlers and analysts to receive decoy pages or broken links instead of malware.
  • A loader that appeared generic enough to be dismissed as commodity adware was actually the common link between unrelated enterprise infections and a much larger pay-per-install distribution network.
  • The YouTube videos were not purely fake lures; they included real gaming optimization content while using download links in descriptions to route viewers into the same infection infrastructure as the SEO-poisoning funnel.
  • Docro Hijacker shows that an older Chrome browser-hijacking technique first seen in 2015 had been re-engineered to bypass modern Secure Preferences integrity protections and was deployed in the wild.
  • ARKTunnel had at least 50 samples spanning a year and multiple fabricated company identity rotations, yet it had no public reporting or dedicated tracking before this investigation.

Unit 42 found a large cybercrime operation, tracked as CL-CRI-1171, that used gaming YouTube channels and fake search results for software downloads to trick people into installing harmful programs. It mainly targeted young gamers, but the same path also led to infections on company computers, including at critical infrastructure and government organizations. The article matters because infections that look minor or ordinary can actually be a doorway for several different harmful programs at once, including tools that let attackers keep access, route traffic through a victim’s computer, or secretly change browser searches for profit.

Cisco Talos is tracking active exploitation of two Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center Software vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316. CVE-2026-20079 is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability with a CVSS score of 10.0 that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute scripts and obtain root access. CVE-2026-20316 has a CVSS score of 5.3 and allows a remote attacker to log in using a low-privileged account, but Talos says it can be combined with other Cisco Secure FMC vulnerabilities to elevate privileges.

Talos identified three clusters of post-compromise activity on FMC instances associated with state-sponsored and crimeware threat actors. UAT-12197 exploited CVE-2026-20079 to deploy a JSP web shell, place a malicious cmd.jar command executor, and query internal databases for user authentication data and credentials. UAT-11823 exploited CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316, used a malicious license.tmp file to establish a Netcat-based reverse shell, exfiltrated managed-device configurations, and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant. UAT-11988, assessed by Talos with high confidence as a ransomware operator, used static credentials linked to CVE-2026-20316 for access and later carried out activity consistent with Qilin ransomware affiliates.

Cisco advises customers to apply already released hotfixes for affected software versions for both CVEs as soon as possible. The article says a comprehensive hardening release containing these hotfixes and fixes for other internally discovered vulnerabilities will be released the following week. Talos also provides detection guidance, including Snort SIDs for CVE-2026-20079, CVE-2026-20316, and related malware, and lists indicators of compromise including web shell and command-executor hashes, attacker IP addresses, and a Cyclops Blink malware hash.

  • The lower-severity CVE-2026-20316 is especially important because Talos says it can be combined with other Cisco Secure FMC vulnerabilities to elevate privileges, and it was used in both the UAT-11823 and UAT-11988 activity clusters.
  • Legitimate FMC functionality became part of the attack path, as both UAT-11823 and UAT-11988 abused package_info.pl and attacker-crafted license.tmp files to execute malicious actions with root privileges.
  • The compromised FMC systems were not just end targets; in the UAT-11988 case, the device was used as a foothold for broader internal reconnaissance, credential harvesting, tunneling, and preparation for endpoint encryption.
  • Detection should not focus only on the two CVEs, because the article provides separate Snort SIDs for the vulnerabilities and for malware, and describes post-compromise artifacts such as JSP web shells, cmd.jar, license.tmp abuse, Netcat reverse shells, SOCKS5 proxying, and Cyclops Blink.

Cisco Talos says attackers are already taking advantage of two security problems in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center software. Organizations using unpatched versions are affected because attackers can get into these systems, gain powerful access, steal information such as credentials and configurations, and use the access to move further into a company’s network. The article describes activity linked to state-sponsored actors and a ransomware operator, including cases involving Cyclops Blink malware and Qilin ransomware, so the stakes include espionage, long-term hidden access, and systems being locked for ransom. Cisco is urging customers to install the available fixes as soon as possible.

Malicious Chrome and Firefox Extensions Steal Crypto Traders’ Session and Wallet Data

Socket researchers found malicious Chrome and Firefox extensions targeting crypto traders by stealing authenticated Axiom Trade and Padre session tokens, wallet-related data, cookies, and app state, then exfiltrating it to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Users and organizations should block the listed extension IDs, revoke affected sessions, rotate credentials, and review trading and wallet activity for unauthorized access.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Socket Threat Research identified six Chrome and Firefox extensions linked by shared code, command-and-control infrastructure, publishing history, cloned crypto trading tools, marketplace artifacts, and targeting of Axiom Trade and Padre users.
  • 02The Chrome extensions J7Tracker and VREO and the Firefox version of VREO contain a byte-identical malicious module that retrieves authenticated user information, wallet-related bundle data, Firebase access tokens, and application state, then sends it to threat actor-controlled Vercel deployments.
  • 03The Firefox extension Orbit Tracker appeared several weeks later with different malicious logic and infrastructure, but it targets the same Axiom data including sBundles, bundleKey, authenticated user information, browser tokens, and cookies.
  • 04The malicious extensions run inside authenticated Axiom Trade and Padre sessions and automatically collect session and wallet-related data without requiring users to intentionally export credentials or wallet information after installation.
  • 05The article recommends blocking confirmed malicious extension IDs, revoking affected Axiom Trade and Padre sessions and authentication tokens, rotating relevant credentials, reviewing wallet and trading activity, and hunting for listed infrastructure such as dcfdc-eight.vercel.app, snipex-iota.vercel.app, and susi.bonto.run.

Socket Threat Research identified six Chrome and Firefox extensions connected by shared code, command-and-control infrastructure, publishing history, cloned crypto trading tools, marketplace artifacts, and targeting of Axiom Trade and Padre users. Four of the extensions, J7Tracker, VREO for Chrome, VREO for Firefox, and Orbit Tracker, are described as malicious because they collect authenticated session and wallet-related data from crypto traders. The Chrome listings were removed in July 2026, while Orbit Tracker later appeared on Mozilla Add-ons and remained live as of publication.

The malicious J7Tracker and VREO extensions contain the same byte-identical module, vamp/axiom-fetch-intercept.js, which retrieves authenticated user information, wallet-related bundle data, Firebase access tokens, and application state. The code runs inside logged-in Axiom Trade and Padre sessions, checks browser storage and Firebase Auth persistence, and sends stolen data to threat actor-controlled Vercel infrastructure using browser navigation. Orbit Tracker uses different logic and infrastructure but targets the same distinctive Axiom data, including sBundles, bundleKey, authenticated user information, browser tokens, and cookies.

The article says the campaign matters because it targets active trading communities handling substantial cryptocurrency volumes, including Axiom and Padre users. The malware does not require users to manually export credentials or wallet data after installation; once the targeted trading platform is open and the needed application state is available, collection occurs automatically. Socket recommends blocking the malicious extension IDs, revoking affected sessions and tokens, rotating credentials, reviewing wallet and trading activity, and hunting for listed infrastructure such as dcfdc-eight.vercel.app, snipex-iota.vercel.app, and susi.bonto.run.

  • The malware used browser navigation rather than normal web requests to send stolen data, which made the destination less obvious from extension permission reviews and avoided controls that apply to fetch, XHR, and WebSocket traffic.
  • The same malicious Axiom and Padre collection module was byte-identical across J7Tracker, VREO for Chrome, and VREO for Firefox, making the listed SHA-256 hash and file path useful for detecting multiple extensions at once.
  • The article identifies behavior as a more durable detection point than marketplace listings because the actors can republish cloned or rebranded crypto extensions under new extension IDs and publisher accounts.
  • Preserving full URLs in DNS, proxy, browser, and EDR telemetry is especially important because the exfiltrated data is encoded directly into URL parameters or paths.
  • The Orbit Tracker extension opened axiom.trade when installed or updated, showing that the extension tried to bring victims into the targeted trading session where its collector could access valuable application data.

Researchers found several Chrome and Firefox add-ons aimed at cryptocurrency traders that secretly collect login and wallet-related information from people using Axiom Trade and Padre. The affected users are traders who installed extensions such as J7Tracker, VREO, or Orbit Tracker and then used those trading sites while logged in. This matters because the stolen information could let criminals take over accounts or help them steal cryptocurrency, and the article says these trading communities handle very large amounts of money.

Censys announced 14 new ways it can find devices and services that are reachable from the public Internet, including building access systems, Amazon Redshift data warehouses, Tailscale relays, and TVT camera systems.   • Organizations already invested in the community-maintained Jamf Pro provider can stay there temporarily, but Jamf recommends considering Jamf Platform when they need Jamf-backed support, maintenance, or roadmap visibility.
  • Jamf’s infrastructure-as-code approach extends beyond deploying management servers and is intended to manage the actual Jamf product configuration surfaces across the environment.
  • The article frames infrastructure as code as unsuitable for every Jamf administrator and specifically limits its recommended audience to teams with version control discipline, DevOps-capable staff, and complexity at scale.

The article explains that Jamf supports managing Apple devices through written, reviewable configuration files using Terraform, instead of relying only on manual changes in the Jamf console. This mainly affects organizations that already use code-based review and deployment practices and manage Apple fleets at scale. In the real world, the benefit is fewer accidental changes, clearer records of who changed what, faster setup of new Jamf environments, and easier rollback if something goes wrong.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a vendor-focused overview of managing Jamf environments with Terraform and a unified API gateway, not a report on a specific incident, vulnerability, patch, or threat activity. It may be useful for teams operating Jamf at scale, but it is evergreen product and best-practice content, so it is low priority for most security professionals.
